title: The Body and the Temporary Nature of Food
english: …people that a man becomes judge, not of outsiders. But God is the judge of all, since he is the Master of all.
On 1 Corinthians 6:1: He reproaches them because, though they had saints who could judge their cases, they were going to law before unbelievers.

On 1 Corinthians 6:2: Having said above, "You judge those inside, but God will judge those outside," he now puts the whole world under the judgment of the saints. Here, they examine the lives of believers in order to correct them; there, they are entrusted with judging the world, not to correct sinful ways but to expose and condemn them. The twelve apostles will judge the twelve tribes (Matthew 19:28), Jews judging Jews, on the evidence of the very prophets the tribes believed in; yet they did not believe, and that is why they rejected Christ. The other holy ones, that is, those from the nations, will condemn those who did not turn away from idols and believe in the true God. So there is no disagreement between the evangelist and the apostle, for Christ spoke in both. It is written, "The queen of the south will rise up and condemn this generation, and the men of Nineveh will rise up and condemn you" (Matthew 12:41–42).

On 1 Corinthians 6:3: Did he not say, "and the world is judged by you"? Here, by "angels" he does not mean angels by nature, but the ministering priests, the teachers of the people, who will very likely be judged by the saints for teaching falsely about Christ. By saying, "how much more the things of this life?" he showed that he was not speaking of angels by nature, but of those who hold an angel's rank and do spiritual work. If he did mean angels in the strict sense, he plainly meant those who rebelled and fell away from God. Priests were indeed called angels, as Malachi says: "The lips of a priest shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is the angel of the Lord of hosts" (Malachi 2:7). So these are the priests we judge, the ones who led the people astray, and likewise those who founded heresies and twisted Christ's teaching.

On 1 Corinthians 6:4: The least member of the church is a better choice than an unbeliever. Yet the apostle seems to have left something unsaid that is plain enough: the more serious charges must be kept for the mature.
On 1 Corinthians 6:7: You show that the devil has beaten you, not only by going to law before unbelievers, but by the very fact that you have lawsuits with one another.
On 1 Corinthians 6:11: He spoke of one working of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit in those who are justified, and so taught that their substance is one.

On 1 Corinthians 6:12–13: By "by anything" he means not a person but a thing, for this is what the passage is about: "Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will do away with both the one and the other."

The second catena form adds: He means a shameful thing and a passion. Speaking about himself, he urges the others to self-control. He knew that their greed came from the belly, for most people will dare anything for the pleasures of the belly, so he teaches that it does no good to be a slave to one's stomach.

"We know that food is for the stomach." The stomach, too, is set apart for food; yet these things are temporary, and God will bring them to an end. After the resurrection, when immortality is given, there will be no more need of food. Why then do you take such pains over temporary things, which breed fornication and shameful pleasures?

On 1 Corinthians 6:14: It is plain that food and eating are temporary. But the body is set apart not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. So the body cannot be temporary; it will be raised to last for ever, after the pattern of Christ.
On 1 Corinthians 6:15: By the body and members of Christ he means the body of those who have believed and been baptized.

On 1 Corinthians 6:16–19: Whatever sin a man commits to feed or clothe his body, he commits to adorn it and supply its needs, and so to honor the body. But the man who joins himself to a prostitute, making his own body one body with her, outrages and dishonors it. Clothes and finery are outside the body, so whoever sins over them sins outside the body. Or again: the slanderer, or the liar, harms and robs others, and a man commits adultery with another man's wife; but the fornicator outrages himself, and the harm of the act passes to no one else. So whatever sin a man commits, he has sinned, but not against his own body, nor has he dishonored his own flesh as the fornicator has. And yet a murderer, staining his hand with blood, also sins against his own body, and so does the slanderer, who bloodies his tongue, as it were, with his abuse. But the fornicator, he says, plunges his whole self into the…

title: Marriage and Self-Control
english: …mire of fornication. So Paul fell in with the common opinion when he said that the other sins are outside the body. Others say the text means this: the fornicator sins against his own body, that is, against the very make-up of his own body, against the very structure of a human being, so to speak, and against the origins of our birth. It is as if he said: stop outraging, by unlawful intercourse, the workshop of nature from which your own body also sprang. Others again say that Paul was eager to show that the sin of fornication is beyond pardon. He had said above, "Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?" and so on, and had shown from this that the fornicator offends against the members of Christ. So he goes on, "Every sin," and the rest. The slanderer, the robber or the grasping man has offended against the person he slandered or wronged, but the fornicator sins against his own body, which is the members of Christ. Once a man has become part of the body of Christ through the adoption the Spirit gives, he will be charged not with fornication only but with impiety as well, since he makes the members of Christ the members of a prostitute and outrages his own body as Christ's temple. That is why he adds, "Or do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God," and so on. In the sin of fornication you sin against the body as against God's temple, and it drives the Holy Spirit away. Not that the other sins go unpunished, for every one of them costs a man the kingdom; but, given the case in hand, he was eager to declare fornication the worst of all. He wanted to tear the passion out by the roots, since the Corinthians were committing it with particular impiety: "It is actually reported," he says, "that there is fornication among you" (1 Corinthians 5:1), and so on.

On 1 Corinthians 6:19–20: The fornicator is guilty of impiety as well, for by outraging his own body he has defiled the temple of the Holy Spirit. He says this because some were committing fornication with contempt, thinking it a small slip, or no slip at all, since Moses did not even mention it in his Ten Commandments. The price is the saving blood of Christ, which he gave as a ransom for us. Glorify God, then, not only in the gift but in the body as well, so that nature, will and gift may all glorify God.
The second catena form adds: "Glorify God, then, in your body and in your spirit." Others have taken "spirit" to mean the soul.

On 1 Corinthians 7:1: He wrote this in reply to the clergy, for it was they who had written to the apostle. He forbade fornication as unlawful, allowed the partnership of marriage as godly and as a release from fornication, and praised continence as the more perfect way.

On 1 Corinthians 7:2–4: He teaches that those joined in marriage have authority over each other rather than over themselves. It is a fine debt for those who live together when, besides the rest of their harmony, they know to pay each other this one as something owed. The apostle stooped so far as a matter of wise management, to cut out fornication, the worst of diseases, by teaching this.

On 1 Corinthians 7:5: Since he had said that they are each other's servants, he goes on, consistently, to say that they must not deprive each other of themselves, except by a godly agreement. Otherwise they may become the cause of each other's fornication, or ruin their authority over each other by parting against each other's will.

On 1 Corinthians 7:6–7: It is in allowance for the nature of the body that I say you should come together again, since I am not saying this to shut out continence for you; I want everyone to be continent, as I am myself.

On 1 Corinthians 7:8–9: He advises widows, and unmarried men who have not taken up virginity, to be continent; but if the flesh got the better of them, to marry. He shows by this that continence is a great thing; yet he allows marriage as a good bond.

On 1 Corinthians 7:10–11: He would not have said that a wife must not separate from her husband about those who separate in order to renounce the world and give themselves to Christ. "Let her be reconciled to her husband, or remain unmarried" is plainly about those who part because of some quarrel. Above he spoke of separation for the sake of continence; here, of separation that comes from bickering. Then he said, "not I but the Lord," because there are things the apostle says on his own, and the Lord did not say everything in person. He means: I charge you with what the Lord already charged in the Gospels about married people, when he said, "What God…

title: Paul's Counsel on Virginity
english: …has joined together, let no man separate" (Matthew 19:6). These words too, "but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried," agree with what the Lord said: "If anyone marries a woman who has been divorced, he commits adultery" (Matthew 5:32), and so does she, if she is married to another.

On 1 Corinthians 7:12: When he says, "I, not the Lord," he is not laying down a law against the Lord's. Some things the Lord said in person; others, about parting from an unbelieving spouse, are said now for the first time by the apostle. And he teaches that unbelief does not overpower faith; rather, the faith of the believing partner sanctifies even the unbeliever.
On 1 Corinthians 7:13: He is not speaking of taking an unbeliever in marriage, but of bearing with an unbeliever.
On 1 Corinthians 7:14: The children are holy: clean, and not defiled even by the unbelief, for in them the parents' faith wins out over the unbelief.

On 1 Corinthians 7:17: To one God assigned the task of saving, to another that of being saved, giving each what each deserved. By "as God has assigned to each" he does not mean having an unbelieving spouse, but bearing with one.

On 1 Corinthians 7:18–24: Circumcision is not good in itself; it was good because God commanded it. Uncircumcision is God's handiwork, not a reward the uncircumcised have earned. Then he says to the slave: do not set your heart on a freedom that will pass; even if you can gain it, make use of your slavery instead. The reward is greater when a man busy in the service of men does not neglect to please God. Let each one remain in the state in which he was called, the slave not chafing at his slavery, the free man not puffed up, for with God there is no difference.

In this respect a believing slave has nothing less than a free man. With God the slave too is seen as free, and has been set free by him. That is what "is the Lord's freedman" means: he has been freed by the Lord. And the man called to the faith as a free man will have nothing more than the slave; he is Christ's slave just as the other is.
That is: do not, for the sake of your needs, live like slaves, without a free man's spirit, courting men, and so abandon the true Master, whose blood bought you.

Grace knows no difference between slavery and mastery. So do not run from slavery as though it were unworthy of the faith; because of it you have no less than anyone else in the faith. And even if you could obtain your freedom, let your concern be rather how you can make better use of what you have, as one whose care is to be free from evil. To show that the free man has no more with Christ on that account, and that the slave is not made less, he adds, for that very reason: "For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was called as a free man is Christ's slave."

On 1 Corinthians 7:25–26: Elsewhere he says, "since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me" (2 Corinthians 13:3); how then does he now say, "I have no command of the Lord"? Who would accept him if he says what the Lord has not commanded him? Plainly he does not mean that he has no command to teach about virginity. He means that he did not receive from God the right to order you to remain virgins, but rather to give his opinion and advise that virginity is good and useful. That is why, as one giving advice, he says "I think" and calls it "good," and leaves the choice of taking it up to his hearers. The thing is pleasing to God, as the Lord too said that some have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom (Matthew 19:12), calling virginity "becoming a eunuch" because the body is left unused. So he says he has no command, and the matter was left to each one's judgment with the words, "Let him who can accept it accept it" (Matthew 19:12). Then, by calling himself trustworthy, he makes plain that what he says is trustworthy and fit to be a command. He says "I think" not because he doubts that virginity is good, but to make sure it is not taken for a command.
On 1 Corinthians 7:28: He showed that he brings in virginity, not to accuse marriage, but to spare the saints; for marriage fills the flesh with birth pains and toil.
The second catena form adds: He is concerned to set them free from the cares of this life, and after saying, "I would spare you," he recommends virginity to spare the saints.

On 1 Corinthians 7:29–31: He gives another reason for preferring virginity, and shows throughout that he does [not] accuse marriage when he prefers holiness. The world is near its end, and we must recognize that what we have we do not really have, since we leave it behind: "so that those who have wives may be as though they had none." If it is good for those who have to have as though they had not, how much better for the virgin not to enter marriage at all? "And those who use this world as though not using it to the full": by this he rules out unmeasured enjoyment, but need…
